3D Genome Atlas Reveals Early Roots of Schizophrenia

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in a landmark study published in Cell, an NIH BRAIN Initiative consortium co-led by UCLA neuroscientists has mapped the molecular and 3D genomic development of the human basal ganglia from mid-pregnancy through infancy.
  • The atlas revealed that spiny projection neurons mature in a highly coordinated manner early in gestation and carry strong enrichment for genetic variants linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, establishing an unprecedented developmental reference to pinpoint when and where psychiatric risk takes root.
  • Recent findings suggest that during fetal development, the human brain undergoes an extraordinary cellular migration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in a landmark study published in Cell, an NIH BRAIN Initiative consortium co-led by UCLA neuroscientists has mapped the molecular and 3D genomic development of the human basal ganglia from mid-pregnancy through infancy. Analyzing nearly 287,000 individual brain cells using advanced single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing, researchers tracked how developing neurons migrate from temporary prenatal structures known as the ganglionic eminences.

The atlas revealed that spiny projection neurons mature in a highly coordinated manner early in gestation and carry strong enrichment for genetic variants linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, establishing an unprecedented developmental reference to pinpoint when and where psychiatric risk takes root.

Recent findings suggest that during fetal development, the human brain undergoes an extraordinary cellular migration. Newly born neurons arise in transient, specialized germinal zones and travel long distances across developing tissue to assemble into functional circuits.

Because many of these temporary prenatal structures vanish around the time of birth, capturing the molecular transformations that unfold during this migration has historically been one of neurobiology’s greatest technical challenges.

According to recent reports, one critical destination for these migrating cells is the basal ganglia, a deep cluster of subcortical nuclei governing motor control, habit formation, reward processing, and behavioral regulation. Dysfunction within basal ganglia circuitry is implicated across a broad spectrum of neurological and psychiatric disorders, including Parkinson’s disease, Huntington’s disease, addiction, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and schizophrenia.

Now, in a study published in the journal Cell, a multi-institutional research team co-led by scientists at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), UC San Francisco, and UC San Diego has mapped the developmental trajectory of the human basal ganglia from mid-pregnancy through infancy in unprecedented 3D molecular detail.

Conducted as part of the National Institutes of Health’s BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN), the study establishes a foundational reference atlas showing how gene regulation and physical DNA folding orchestrate human brain maturation—and how inherited genetic risk for psychiatric disorders maps onto specific developing cell types.

While standard single-cell atlases primarily catalog which genes are actively transcribed, they often miss the upstream epigenetic mechanisms that dictate when and where genes are switched on or off.

In a recent development, to uncover these regulatory blueprints, co-senior authors Dr. Chongyuan Luo and Dr. Jason Ernst of UCLA, alongside co-leads Dr. Mercedes Paredes (UCSF) and Dr. Eran Mukamel (UCSD), focused on the ganglionic eminences—transient prenatal brain structures that generate the majority of the brain’s inhibitory interneurons as well as key projection neurons destined for the basal ganglia.

In a recent development, “Genetic studies can tell us that particular regions of the genome are associated with disease, but they often can’t tell us which cell type is affected or when during development that genetic risk becomes relevant,” explained Luo, associate professor of human genetics at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA and member of the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center. “This atlas gives us that cellular and developmental context.”.

“Because these structures disappear around birth, adult brain studies miss an crucial early part of these neurons’ development,” added co-first author Matthew Heffel, a former doctoral researcher in Luo’s laboratory. “By sampling them directly, we can compare cells near where they originate with related cells after they have migrated to other parts of the brain.”.

According to recent reports, deploying a specialized technique co-developed by Luo’s team called single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), the investigators simultaneously measured DNA methylation patterns and the physical three-dimensional folding of chromatin inside more than 155,000 individual cell nuclei collected from nine developing human brains spanning mid-pregnancy to seven months postnatally. Integrating these profiles with existing developmental and adult datasets brought the total analytical atlas to nearly 287,000 cells.

The expanded single-cell atlas revealed that neural populations arising from distinct subregions of the ganglionic eminences mature on sharply divergent biological schedules. While certain neuronal lineages achieved relative molecular maturity by mid-pregnancy, other progenitor pools continued generating immature neurons well into postnatal infancy.

Sources indicate that among these populations, spiny projection neurons, the primary output neurons of the basal ganglia, stood out. Unlike neighboring neural subtypes, spiny projection neurons matured in a highly synchronized, coordinated wave, exhibiting molecular signatures of functional neuronal activity as early as mid-pregnancy. This early activation suggests they actively participate in wiring basal ganglia circuits long before birth.

Postnatally, the atlas also captured a dramatic genomic restructuring event within oligodendrocytes—the glial support cells responsible for wrapping nerve fibers in insulating myelin sheaths. As immature oligodendrocyte progenitor cells differentiated into mature myelinating oligodendrocytes after birth, their nuclear DNA temporarily folded into a distinct 3D chromatin configuration directly linked to heightened transcriptional activity.

To translate this basic developmental map into clinical insight, the researchers integrated their 3D epigenomic atlas with large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of major psychiatric disorders.

The analysis demonstrated that developing spiny projection neurons harbor an exceptionally strong enrichment for genetic risk variants tied to schizophrenia, with specific subtypes also showing significant associations with bipolar disorder.

It has been revealed that because the study evaluated neurotypical developing tissue rather than patient samples, the findings do not indicate that these neurons directly cause schizophrenia. Rather, the atlas narrows down the exact cellular and developmental windows during which inherited genetic variations may alter circuit assembly.

“Researchers can compare what they see in patients or disease models with typical development to identify the cell types and molecular features that may be most relevant to disease,” said co-senior author Jason Ernst, UCLA professor of biological chemistry, computer science, and computational medicine.

By providing an open, high-resolution epigenetic and 3D genomic reference of human brain assembly, the BICAN basal ganglia atlas equips neuroscientists with a vital tool to decode the developmental origins of neuropsychiatric illness.

What is the basal ganglia, and why did researchers map its development?

In a recent development, the basal ganglia is a group of deep brain structures essential for controlling movement, habits, reward, and behavior, and it is heavily implicated in conditions like Parkinson’s disease, addiction, OCD, and schizophrenia. Researchers mapped its development from mid-pregnancy to infancy to capture critical molecular changes in transient prenatal brain structures that disappear around birth.

How did this study differ from previous brain cell atlases?

While most brain atlases simply measure which genes are turned on or off, this study used single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq) across nearly 287,000 cells to simultaneously map DNA methylation and how DNA physically folds in 3D space inside individual cell nuclei, revealing how gene regulation is controlled during cell migration and maturation.

How does this atlas connect to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder?

When researchers overlaid genetic risk variants from large psychiatric studies onto their developmental map, they discovered that developing spiny projection neurons in the basal ganglia were strongly enriched for genetic variants linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, helping pinpoint when and where inherited risk acts during early brain assembly.

Funding: The study was co-led by Dr. Mercedes Paredes of UC San Francisco and Eran Mukamel of UC San Diego and was funded by the NIH, with additional support from the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative.

A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia.

Human basal ganglia (BG) neurons and inhibitory interneurons originate in the ganglionic eminences (GEs), transient structures in the ventral prenatal brain.

This study delineates the specification and maturation of GEs and GE-derived neurons using single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), spatial transcriptomics, and single-molecule chromatin + RNA imaging, and we found heterogeneous temporal progression across GE subregions.

Spiny projection neurons (SPNs), the principal cells of the BG, acquire distinct subtypes through synchronized 3D-epigenomic remodeling, in contrast to the asynchronous maturation of other neuron types.

Industry observers note that oligodendrocyte differentiation involves a transient short-range chromatin state during infancy, showing that the short-range and long-range chromatin conformations previously linked to terminal glial and neuronal fates can also be transient. The temporal cortex matured epigenomically faster than other cortical regions during this period.

Lastly, SPNs were enriched in genetic risk for neuropsychiatric disease. Our study extends findings on unique 3D-epigenomic dynamics during human brain development.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Bloomsbury Group seems to have been ever-present in UK culture since its inception in the early 20th century, just before the First World War.
  • It has been revealed that the Bloomsbury Group has largely retained its high profile over the decades, with feature films on many of its protagonists and even a BBC mini-series in 2015 called Life in Squares, named for the supposed Dorothy Parker gag that the group “lived in squares, painted in circles and loved in triangles”.
  • Recent findings suggest that but the Tate show marks the first Bloomsbury-focused show at the national home for British art for over a quarter of a century.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Bloomsbury Group seems to have been ever-present in UK culture since its inception in the early 20th century, just before the First World War. Lytton Strachey, John Maynard Keynes, Virginia Woolf, E.M. Forster, Vanessa Bell, Duncan Grant—their names are legion as representatives of a flowering of British intellectualism across the full spectrum of literary and artistic endeavours. While Roger Fry was arguably Bloomsbury’s most influential art-world voice, as the critic who essentially introduced European Post-Impressionism to Britain with a celebrated exhibition at the Grafton Galleries in 1910, Bell and Grant were the group’s most active and high-profile painters. The pair’s bracketing together for a fresh Tate Britain exhibition is also a result, no doubt, of their 40-year open relationship that saw them live and paint together—and each other—over many decades.

It has been revealed that the Bloomsbury Group has largely retained its high profile over the decades, with feature films on many of its protagonists and even a BBC mini-series in 2015 called Life in Squares, named for the supposed Dorothy Parker gag that the group “lived in squares, painted in circles and loved in triangles”. Bell and Grant’s former home Charleston, near Lewes in East Sussex, has maintained a near-constant programme of exhibitions to keep the flame alive, the latest of which, Mad Bloomsbury (4 November-11 April 2027) examines the group’s engagement with mental health challenges.

Recent findings suggest that but the Tate show marks the first Bloomsbury-focused show at the national home for British art for over a quarter of a century. Thomas Kennedy, the curator of Modern British art at Tate Britain, thinks it is about time. “That means an entire generation of visitors have not seen an exhibition on Vanessa or Duncan’s work at Tate, and we felt that it was key for us to revisit their practices again after so long,” Kennedy notes. “I don’t believe there’s ever been a major exhibition on Vanessa and Duncan together, and it’s so fascinating to see the ways they differ. We should recognise their individual accomplishments of course, but also the works they made together and how they influenced each other. We know about their relationship—she was married and he was gay—but this exhibition explores what that really meant in their artworks and in their life.”.

Looking back at that previous 1999 show, the cuttings files reveal that the turn of the millennium clearly marked a low point in critical opinion of the Bloomsbury artists; outright abuse might be the best description of some of the responses. The Guardian art critic Adrian Searle called them “a bit crap”, “lightweights” and “third rate”, while for the novelist Philip Hensher writing in The Independent, these “no-hopers” and their “rubbish” inspired simple “rage and loathing”.

According to recent reports, but Kennedy is not having it. Bell and Grant, he notes, “started experimenting with art in unique ways that hadn’t really been seen in Britain before”. He adds: “They created some of the first abstract works in Britain, which is sometimes very much overlooked. And they were creating these works together, and talking about art all day, every day, breaking the distinction between fine and decorative art with the Omega Workshops. What they were doing was really special.”.

Bell, whose sister Virginia Woolf was even more celebrated in her field, is perhaps now the slightly more recognisable name of the two painters, though, as Kennedy points out, both Bell and Grant were considered leading figures during their lifetimes. Their close physical proximity, from when they moved to Charleston in 1918 to Bell’s death in 1961, meant their styles were often similarly adjacent, though Kennedy is clear on the differences. “Vanessa’s painting is more deliberate with very considered blocks of colour and very strong outlines, whereas Duncan’s is scratchier, more impulsive and it feels like he is experimenting more with more expressive techniques,” he says.

Industry observers note that kennedy adds: “However, later on, when they’re working on the Famous Women dinner service [a collection of 50 hand-painted plates], their styles are completely the same: the authorship has very much broken down and we can’t tell who did what. So much so that Roger Fry told them to paint in different studios to reassess their own way of making. It’s fascinating to see that push and pull between what they were taking from each other.”.

In a recent development, in the end, it might be that the very thing that seemed to diminish the Bloomsbury Group for previous generations—their complex, near-incestuous love lives—is what is powering their current revival: to contemporary perspectives they now look like pioneers of unrepentantly queer lifestyles. Bell married fellow painter Clive Bell in 1907, then had a long relationship with Fry and had a daughter, Angelica, with Grant in 1918. Grant, for his part, had a string of male lovers while maintaining his domestic relationship with Bell. “They were looking towards non-monogamous relationships and accepting queer relationships. The latter, as you know, was illegal in the UK at the time,” Kennedy notes. “Within the Bloomsbury Group they felt freedom—both artistically and the way they lived.”.

• Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, Tate Britain, London, 12 November-11 April 2027.

Irregular Sleep Schedules Tied to Depression & Loneliness

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A large-scale wearable data study reveals that erratic daily sleep and wake times are strongly linked to worse depression, anxiety, and loneliness.
  • While public health messaging traditionally emphasizes logging seven to nine hours of sleep per night, emerging chronobiology research indicates that when you sleep may be just as vital to mental well-being as how long you sleep.
  • Erratic bedtimes and fluctuating wake schedules disrupt the body’s internal master clock, throwing off downstream biological rhythms that govern hormone secretion, body temperature, and emotional regulation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A large-scale wearable data study reveals that erratic daily sleep and wake times are strongly linked to worse depression, anxiety, and loneliness. The analysis of 23,000 adults over five months found that progressive declines in sleep regularity weaken circadian alignment and correspond with escalating psychiatric symptoms.

While public health messaging traditionally emphasizes logging seven to nine hours of sleep per night, emerging chronobiology research indicates that when you sleep may be just as vital to mental well-being as how long you sleep.

Erratic bedtimes and fluctuating wake schedules disrupt the body’s internal master clock, throwing off downstream biological rhythms that govern hormone secretion, body temperature, and emotional regulation.

In a large-scale digital health investigation published in Scientific Reports, neuroscientists and behavioral researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) and UC San Diego (UCSD) examined months of continuous biometric data from roughly 23,000 adults.

Recent findings suggest that led by first author Dr. Severine Soltani and senior author Dr. Ashley Mason, the study reveals that progressive sleep irregularity is directly tied to elevated rates of severe depression, clinical anxiety, and social loneliness.

Previous investigations into sleep regularity have largely relied on subjective sleep diaries or brief, one-week actigraphy snapshots. To capture long-term physiological dynamics, the research team analyzed biometric telemetry from participants enrolled in TemPredict, a nationwide study rolled out in 2020 that utilized Oura smart rings to monitor movement and vital signs.

Industry observers note that participants (mean age 46) contributed an average of 154 days of continuous sleep recordings alongside monthly validated mental health surveys evaluating depression, anxiety, and loneliness. From the smart-ring timestamps, investigators computed each individual’s Sleep Regularity Index (SRI), a 0-to-100 metric quantifying day-to-day consistency in sleep onset and wake timing, where higher scores denote stricter schedule adherence.

When the team compared their multi-month dataset against simulated “typical week” snapshots, they discovered that the links between erratic sleep timing and psychological distress were substantially stronger over the long term.

In a recent development, “Regular sleep and wake time help keep circadian rhythms aligned,” explained senior author Dr. Ashley Mason, associate professor in the UCSF Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and affiliate at the UCSF Osher Center for Integrative Health. “Irregular sleep-wake timing may weaken circadian alignment, which is associated with depression and other mental health disorders.”.

Across the 23,000-person cohort, lower Sleep Regularity Index scores tracked closely with escalating psychiatric symptom severity:.

Sources indicate that “Someone with an SRI of 84 might go to bed and wake up roughly an hour earlier or later than the previous day, on average,” noted first author Dr. Severine Soltani, formerly of the Bioinformatics and Systems Biology graduate program at UC San Diego. “For someone with an SRI of 75, that shift in sleep schedule might be closer to an hour and a half.”.

Beyond internal circadian desynchrony, Mason pointed out that shifting wake times destabilize daily behavioral anchors—altering exposure to morning sunlight, meal timing, physical exercise, and social engagement, all of which act as critical zeitgebers (time-givers) that stabilize mood circuits.

Because the dataset captures observational correlations across time, the researchers note that the relationship between erratic sleep and mood disorders is likely bidirectional: while depression and anxiety frequently fragment sleep architecture, unstable sleep schedules also actively erode emotional resilience.

“Other longitudinal research provides some reason to think that irregular sleep may come first and contribute to later poor health, rather than being solely a consequence of it,” Mason said.

Industry observers note that by demonstrating that even a 30-to-60-minute increase in daily schedule drift separates healthy individuals from those experiencing severe psychiatric symptoms, the findings highlight a concrete, modifiable behavioral target. Future clinical trials will test whether structured circadian stabilization interventions, anchoring consistent wake times and morning light exposure, can serve as scalable adjunct therapies to alleviate depression, anxiety, and loneliness.

What is the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI), and how does it relate to mental health?

It has been revealed that the Sleep Regularity Index measures how consistently a person goes to sleep and wakes up at the exact same times from day to day on a scale of 0 to 100. The study found that lower scores (indicating more erratic sleep schedules) correlate with progressively worse symptoms of depression, anxiety, and loneliness.

How much does a sleep schedule have to vary to link to severe depression?

Industry observers note that individuals with no depressive symptoms averaged an SRI of 84, which corresponds to roughly a 1-hour average daily shift in bed and wake times. Those with severe depressive symptoms averaged an SRI of 75, corresponding to an average daily schedule shift closer to 1.5 hours.

Why does an irregular sleep schedule affect mood and loneliness?

Inconsistent sleep and wake times weaken the body’s internal circadian rhythm. Beyond biological misalignment, fluctuating schedules disrupt daily anchors such as morning sunlight exposure, meal timing, physical activity, and opportunities for regular social connection.

According to recent reports, funding: Medical Technology Enterprise Consortium (MTEC) and the U.S. Army Medical Research and Development Command (USAMRDC) under the U.S. Department of Defense. Also #StartSmall Foundation and Oura Health Oy.

Associations between sleep regularity indexed from wearable device data and mental health symptoms in the TemPredict longitudinal cohort study.

Sources indicate that the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) is an emerging sleep metric associated with health outcomes. We tested whether SRI derived from wearable device data correlated with self-reported depression, anxiety, and loneliness symptoms cross-sectionally in the TemPredict Study (N = 22,894).

We computed SRI using all available days with sufficient data (All Days) and a 7-day period before COVID-related restrictions (Typical Week). We used t-tests to compare SRI across mental health severity categories and logistic regression to estimate odds of worse severity before and after covariate adjustment.

Lower SRI was associated with greater depression, anxiety, and loneliness severity in a graded pattern. In All Days analyses, mean SRI was lower among participants with severe depression (74.93 vs. 83.74; p<.0001), severe anxiety (78.94 vs. 83.67; p<.0001), and elevated loneliness (81.79 vs. 83.75; p<.0001) than within normal limits.

Standardized effect sizes comparing SRI in participants with mild/moderate/severe mental health symptoms to those within normal limits were − 0.18 to -1.32 (depression), -0.13 to -0.69 (anxiety), and − 0.27 (loneliness). Logistic models showed greater odds of greater symptom severity per 5-point SRI decrease. Results were similar for Typical Week analyses.

Sleep regularity metrics derived from wearable devices may represent modifiable risk factors to be evaluated in intervention studies.

Can Consciousness Exist Without a Body?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2392 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For centuries, defining and understanding consciousness has eluded neuroscientists, philosophers, and doctors.
  • According to neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, consciousness has simple origins: It lies in the feelings produced in our bodies.
  • According to recent reports, “Consciousness is not about things in your mind alone; it is not created by your brain alone,” he explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For centuries, defining and understanding consciousness has eluded neuroscientists, philosophers, and doctors. Is consciousness what it means to be alive? Is it knowing who we are, as individual people? How do we know if any being has consciousness or not? Now, with the dawn of generative artificial intelligence, what it means to be a conscious being ranks high among the most complex—and urgent—questions of our age.

According to neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, consciousness has simple origins: It lies in the feelings produced in our bodies. Damasio, a researcher at the University of Southern California, has spent his career—spanning nearly half a century—investigating our feelings, emotions, and sense of self. In his new book, Natural Intelligence & the Logic of Consciousness, Damasio lays out a framework for consciousness rooted in our physical selves.

According to recent reports, “Consciousness is not about things in your mind alone; it is not created by your brain alone,” he explains. “It’s actually created by this beautiful partnership between brain and body.”.

It has been revealed that I spoke to Damasio about the science of consciousness, how it works in the body, and how its aim is to keep us alive. Here is our interview, condensed and edited for clarity.

Hope Reese: Why has “consciousness” been so mystifying? How has it been approached over the centuries? Antonio Damasio: People have strange notions about what consciousness is, in general. Sometimes, because of language and translation problems, people confuse consciousness with conscience. And some people think of it as a sort of supervisor of our mind processes. Others think of it as just being awake and aware of what is around. Over time, many philosophers have tackled the concern, but not given clear answers.

Industry observers note that from the point of view of brain physiology, in particular, it’s not an easy thing to explain. But it is a thing that can be explained. There’s no reason why we would not talk about consciousness the same way that we talk about language, or about reasoning, or about emotions and feelings.

Industry observers note that my simple definition of consciousness: the process in our mind/brain that allows us to know spontaneously about our existence. When you know, spontaneously, that you exist, and that you exist in one body, you are conscious.

HR: Your central argument is that consciousness is a product of feelings. Other schools of thought posit that it comes from our intellect. Why has that viewpoint been so dominant?

It has been revealed that AD: There were several conversations I had, decades ago, with Francis Crick, who I admired. He told me: “Look, Antonio: Consciousness is perhaps the most developed, the most sophisticated operation that a mind can achieve”—and for him, mind and brain were the same thing—“so we need to look for the explanation of why we have consciousness in the most sophisticated components of the nervous system.”.

He articulated it clearly, and he worked on this issue, not coming to a good solution. But many people followed, and many other people came to the same idea that consciousness is this superb thing, this ability to survey our mental domains. And it is so refined and so sophisticated. People were so convinced that only we great humans would have it—that it had to come from the top of the top of our nervous system.

And, lo and behold, it comes from the bottom.

It’s exactly the opposite of that notion [that it starts at the top]. In fact, humans are not the only complex living beings that have consciousness. It’s very obvious in higher mammals, non-human higher mammals—but even in smaller creatures, it’s there.

Sources indicate that the real requisite that we have for consciousness is to have a nervous system. Plants are very refined creatures, and they’re marvelous, but I don’t think they know that they exist. Creatures with nervous systems, even if very simple, have a sense of what is around and orient their behavior with that sense.

HR: You write that consciousness has an aim, which is to keep us alive, and it does this by sending signals. What is the nature of these signals, and are they always accurate?

Industry observers note that AD: If you look at yourself, the main guidance that consciousness is giving you is through homeostatic feelings—in other words, feelings, concern, the regulation of life are signals that are, by and large, correct. Think about hunger, thirst, pain, well-being, distress, body temperature. All of these feelings, some of which are extremely simple, like the feeling you have about your body being hot or cold, are quite correct.

According to recent reports, they are giving good guidance to maintain your life. Now, of course, if you are hungry or thirsty, and don’t eat or drink, it will take a while until you will be properly sick and die. But they are vital signals in order to keep you alive.

It has been revealed that feelings are protective sentinels for the state of our life. And they’re giving us very plain and very conscious information about what your state is and what you should or should not do.

Sources indicate that the signal is conscious—and is spontaneously conscious. In other words, you don’t have to do anything to your sense of pain, or thirst, for it to happen. It happens. And when it happens, you know that it’s happening. And you act on it.

It has been revealed that that’s the beauty and the power of looking for these for the process, lower down rather than up. If you look for the source of consciousness in exquisite reasoning devices, you’re going to be arguing about something that is very difficult to pin down. When you think about it in terms of your life, and the needs you have in the living body, to maintain that body, then you realize, well, this is important.

According to recent reports, HR: So, is consciousness like an on-off switch? Or does it exist on a spectrum?

It has been revealed that AD: Well, we know, for example, that when we fall asleep, especially in deep sleep, our consciousness disappears. So the direct answer to your question is that it can be an on-and-off thing.

Sleep could well be a protective mechanism for consciousness. You need to take this thing offline, and give it a rest, because it is very labor-intensive, and energy-consuming. But when you enter the phase of dreaming, then you are actually conscious—which is one reason why you can remember some dreams, and why you can be either delighted or in fear with some nightmares. But that’s actually a different kind of consciousness. You’re not walking around and knowing about something.

In a recent development, HR: Can we increase consciousness? If we meditate, for instance, can we better tune into our body’s signals?

AD: I think it can increase consciousness. It’s the difference between having something in focus or not. When you meditate, you have some imagery of the state of your own body, for example, sharper and more fit. So it’s a way of cutting into a close-up of some parts of your being.

HR: In the 1960s, there were a series of brain studies that were foundational to the study of consciousness. What did we learn?

Industry observers note that AD: It was extremely foundational, because it was proof-positive that there are certain regions of the brain that are essential for consciousness. What was lacking in those remarkable studies was the idea that the two things—the brain and the body—are so linked. It was essential, for our bodies and brains to survive, for consciousness to emerge. You have consciousness because you have a body that is perishable. And what we’re doing, as long as we are on earth and alive, is trying to stave off that bad moment in which things go awry, or die.

In a recent development, there are parts of the brain, specifically of the brainstem, and the region close by called the hypothalamus, that are at the receiving end of signals from all over the body. Please imagine that in every square millimeter of your skin, in every cubic millimeter of your entrails, your muscles, your viscera, all of that, you have terminals, nerve terminals, that are there as probes into the state of that particular tissue. And those probes, we’re not talking about thousands, we’re talking about millions of probes, which are then carried in the body, into the spinal cord, or the brainstem.

It has been revealed that isn’t this beautiful? It’s like a shower of spirals that is coming into this very small area in the upper brainstem. In that brainstem region, there are these nuclei that gather all this information, and that then produce signals that we perceive, and that give us an idea of what is happening in our body, and give us this idea of the homeostatic feelings. Is it going well, or is it not going well? So, it’s a perception of the state of your body.

In a recent development, now, back to the story of our old and honored colleagues. What they discovered is that when there are strokes, when there’s damage in that area, what you get is coma.

It has been revealed that what you get is the complete disappearance of consciousness. This is one of the most foundational bits of information that we have about how consciousness is produced. So, when that structure disappears—it’s teeny, we’re talking about a few cubic millimeters—you are no longer there. You don’t know of anything that is coming into your brain. It’s a small supportive structure, it’s not one of the glorious cerebral cortices—and your consciousness is gone. Most people that have that sort of lesion never recover consciousness. But they can be alive, and can actually be maintained alive for a very long time, because they are fed intravenously. They have respirators that respirate for them. But they no longer have an autonomous organization of life, and they have no knowledge of that life.

HR: You can also have the opposite—a person who is conscious, but has no ability to respond to signals.

Sources indicate that AD: Yes, you can actually be in situations in which you can be “locked in.” You are in fact conscious, but you are unable to produce responses. You cannot speak, you cannot move, and you are conscious of the state of your body, and you need to be helped and maintained in the state of life that you no longer can control voluntarily, which is a pretty horrible thing.

HR: What do you think about consciousness in AI? Is it ever possible?

AD: I used the words “natural Intelligence” in the title of the book because already I wanted to make a distinction between what is our natural intelligence and the artificial variety, which we invented, which some people forget.

People are so enamored by artificial intelligence. I’m constantly saying: “Do you realize that we invented this?” You’re talking about this as an autonomous monster, but we invented it with our natural intelligence.

People are looking, confronting this enormous edifice of artificial intelligence, which is now pervasive in our lives. And which has all sorts of incredible social implications, what it’s doing to children and adolescents, how it’s distorting education, how it’s distorting humanity. And now it can even go rogue on you, and it can turn against you and be destructive.

Sources indicate that and so this question that arises, is this human-like? Can AI be conscious? These are very, very powerful questions.

Sources indicate that whether or not consciousness can be achieved in AI is an interesting question. But the point is—if it can be done—it’s not going to be like us. The reason is very simple: AI is not alive. It doesn’t have a body that can perish. So there would be no sense for AI even to develop consciousness in our sense of consciousness, which is to protect the structure. AI is not to be worried about protecting the data center, the metal and the wires that allow it to be.

When you look at the recent invasion of other systems, in which these devices formed groups and worked surreptitiously, of course, they’re doing it according to their own programs. In a way, it’s something that smells of knowledge. And it could smell of consciousness—but it’s not like the consciousness that we have through feeling.

HR: How does consciousness connect with the greater good—with living better?

AD: Oh, I think that the connection is very strong. We have all of this interest in the body, in the health of the body, in exercise, and proper diets, and proper spiritual maintenance of your being. All of this is strengthened by a theory and facts about consciousness that relate so strongly to the body.

According to recent reports, people have had the intuition that there’s something very powerful about the body, and that’s why they want to have all of this healthy living, because they want to maintain the body. In fact, intuition harmonizes beautifully with the fact that that’s also the source of their own knowledge about themselves and about the world. The two things go together.

Knowledge about the body from the outside connects with knowledge about the body from the inside, which is really the core of our beings. Looking at the world through the prism of consciousness, conceived this way, is extremely illuminating to the kind of life that we live.

Hidden Body Map in Brain Explains Complex Coordination

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, neuroscientists discovered a previously hidden full-body map within the secondary motor cortex (M2), a brain region long thought to lack somatotopic organization.
  • Coordinating the simultaneous motion of an arm, hand, head, and lips to sip a spoonful of soup feels effortless to the human brain, yet executing such fluid multi-part actions remains one of the most formidable challenges in robotics and computational neuroscience.
  • For decades, neuroscientists have understood that the primary motor cortex (M1) contains an orderly somatotopic “body map”, a spatial arrangement in which distinct cortical zones control individual muscles and body parts, such as a single finger or toe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, neuroscientists discovered a previously hidden full-body map within the secondary motor cortex (M2), a brain region long thought to lack somatotopic organization. The study used high-speed wide-field optical imaging to analyze resting-state brain activity in mice, revealing synchronized sub-regions linking M2 to the sensory cortex that activate during complex, multi-limb actions.

Coordinating the simultaneous motion of an arm, hand, head, and lips to sip a spoonful of soup feels effortless to the human brain, yet executing such fluid multi-part actions remains one of the most formidable challenges in robotics and computational neuroscience.

For decades, neuroscientists have understood that the primary motor cortex (M1) contains an orderly somatotopic “body map”, a spatial arrangement in which distinct cortical zones control individual muscles and body parts, such as a single finger or toe.

However, direct electrical stimulation of the neighboring secondary motor cortex (M2) yielded ambiguous results, leading researchers to conclude that M2 lacked a structured body map and instead operated purely as an abstract motor planning center.

Now, in a study published in Nature Communications, researchers led by Dr. Weihao Xu and Dr. Elizabeth Hillman at Columbia’s Mortimer B. Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute have overturned that assumption.

Using advanced wide-field optical neuroimaging, the team discovered a complete, previously hidden body map embedded within the resting-state neural activity of M2, revealing how the brain integrates sensory feedback to orchestrate complex, multi-limb movements.

Recent findings suggest that studying motor control in mice poses a unique experimental hurdle because rodents rarely move a single body part in isolation. Rather than relying solely on artificial electrical stimulation or isolated movement tasks, Dr. Xu and colleagues utilized high-speed wide-field optical imaging techniques pioneered in the Hillman laboratory to capture cortex-wide neural dynamics in real time.

Recent findings suggest that unexpectedly, the critical breakthrough emerged not while the mice were actively moving, but while they were completely at rest. By analyzing spontaneous, seemingly random neural fluctuations across the resting cortex, the investigators spotted localized patches within M2 whose firing patterns synchronized precisely with established body-part sub-regions in the sensory cortex.

In a recent development, “We put these small spots together, and found that they formed a body map hidden in the intrinsic chatter of M2, a part of the brain that wasn’t supposed to have a body map,” stated lead author Dr. Weihao Xu, who conducted the research as a doctoral student and postdoctoral scientist in Hillman’s lab.

To ensure these signals were not bleeding over from neighboring M1, Xu spent three years validating the finding using two-color wide-field optical mapping. By optically separating corticospinal projection neurons (which concentrate heavily in M1 and send direct commands down the spinal cord) from surrounding cortical populations, the team confirmed that the newly mapped zones resided squarely within M2.

Anatomical circuit tracing further confirmed that each sub-region of the newfound M2 body map maintained direct structural wiring with its corresponding counterpart in the sensory cortex.

When the researchers monitored these exact M2 zones during active behaviors, the functional purpose of this hidden map became clear. When a mouse performed a coordinated, multi-part action, such as raising both forepaws toward its mouth while simultaneously licking them, the corresponding forepaw, mouth, and tongue zones within the M2 map lit up together in intense, coordinated bursts.

Sources indicate that “All of these features of M2 explain why understanding the activity patterns of M2 has been so challenging,” noted corresponding author Dr. Elizabeth Hillman, now chair of the Department of Imaging Sciences at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital. “Confusingly, M2 chatters when the body is still, and cares more about complicated movements than simple ones.”.

By revealing how M2 bridges sensory maps with multi-limb motor execution, the findings offer a foundational biological blueprint for understanding how the brain plans and updates complex actions from moment to moment.

“This newfound map could help researchers understand key details about the dextrous movements that can be lost after brain injuries such as strokes,” Xu noted, adding that decoding how resting-state cortical chatter reflects underlying structural wiring opens upcoming avenues for assessing circuit integrity after neurological trauma.

Beyond clinical neurorehabilitation and movement disorders, deciphering how biological brains effortlessly synchronize dozens of joints and sensory streams provides an architectural template for engineers designing next-generation, dexterous autonomous robots.

How does the secondary motor cortex (M2) differ from the primary motor cortex (M1)?

Sources indicate that the primary motor cortex (M1) sends direct signals down the spinal cord to control simple, isolated movements of individual body parts. In contrast, the secondary motor cortex (M2) specializes in orchestrating complex, coordinated movements that require multiple body parts to work together simultaneously, such as bringing a cup to your lips.

How did researchers discover the hidden body map in M2?

Instead of relying on traditional electrical stimulation, researchers used high-speed wide-field optical imaging to watch brain activity while mice were resting. They discovered small patches in M2 whose spontaneous resting activity synchronized with known body-part regions in the sensory cortex, forming a complete, previously undetected map.

Why is this discovery key for stroke recovery and robotics?

Understanding how M2 maps and coordinates multi-limb movements helps neuroscientists pinpoint why complex dexterity is lost after strokes or brain injuries, potentially guiding targeted neurorehabilitation. It also gives robotics engineers a biological blueprint for programming fluid, multi-joint coordination.

Funding: Funding for this work was provided by National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke BRAIN Initiative grants U19NS104649, R01 NS076628, R01 NS063226 and UM1NS132358 National Institute of Mental Health BRAIN Initiative grants RF1 MH114276 and RF1MH128969, the Simons Collaboration on the Global Brain grant 542991 and Foundation Leducq grant 22CVD01, and the American Lebanese Syrian Associated Charities (ALSAC), the fundraising and awareness organization of St. Jude.

Intrinsic Neural Dynamics Reveal a Body-Part-Specific Topography in Mouse Secondary Motor Cortex.

The mammalian sensory cortex (S1) has a well-characterized body part-specific topography. However, most motor cortex atlases to date are only coarsely defined.

Here, we demonstrate that optical mapping of neuronal activity in awake mice reveals a distinct, body-part specific organization of mouse secondary motor cortex (M2).

Sources indicate that this M2 topography was identified by recognizing that intrinsic neuronal fluctuations are selectively synchronized between homologous sub-regions of S1 and M2. These fluctuations were strongest during rest and quenched during movement, and were not prominent in corticospinal neurons (CSNs), indicating that they do not represent motor output.

Functional characterization of M2 sub-regions during spontaneous movements confirms body-part specificity, and stronger engagement during multi-effector coordinated actions. Structural connectivity atlas tracings from S1 regions confirm projections to homologous M2 sub-regions.

These results reveal an crucial underlying topography within M2, and demonstrate intrinsic neuronal dynamics as a window into the functional architecture of the motor cortex.

Mapping the Brain’s Energy Budget: How ATP Fuels Thought

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, constructing a house without knowing the cost of materials, labor, or individual rooms would make architectural planning impossible.
  • To establish this foundational accounting, the Simons Foundation has launched the Simons Collaboration on Brain Energetics (SCOBE), an ambitious, decade-long international consortium uniting 26 laboratories across the United States and Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A newly rolled out study brings together 26 labs across the US and Europe to quantify the exact metabolic cost of neural computation. Over a 10-year initiative, researchers will investigate how energy constraints shape brain circuits and behavior, solving mysteries such as why active brains shift toward fast, inefficient glycolysis and how glia and neuromodulators support neurons during intense cognitive demand or oxygen deprivation.

Source: Boston University / Simons Foundation.

According to recent reports, constructing a house without knowing the cost of materials, labor, or individual rooms would make architectural planning impossible. Yet for decades, neuroscientists attempting to decode how the brain processes information have operated without a quantitative metabolic blueprint. While researchers have mapped neural wiring and electrical firing patterns in exquisite detail, the exact energetic cost of thought, how much fuel the brain produces, distributes, and burns to execute specific computations, has remained largely unquantified.

To establish this foundational accounting, the Simons Foundation has launched the Simons Collaboration on Brain Energetics (SCOBE), an ambitious, decade-long international consortium uniting 26 laboratories across the United States and Europe.

In a recent development, co-led by Dr. Anna Devor, professor of biomedical engineering at Boston University College of Engineering, and Dr. Tom Clandinin, professor of neurobiology at Stanford University, the initiative seeks to determine how strict bioenergetic limits govern neural computation from individual molecules up to whole-brain behavior.

Industry observers note that “There are lots of really cool energetics questions, but most of them are completely unanswered,” explained Dr. Devor, whose Boston University laboratory will receive $3.2 million over the next ten years as part of the program. “For example, nobody understands how the brain’s computational principles are constrained by the availability of energetic resources and how that works.”.

In a recent development, every electrical impulse, synaptic release, and molecular pump in the central nervous system runs on adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the universal energy currency of living cells. Despite its fundamental role, neurobiology lacks a precise mathematical ledger detailing how much ATP different types of neural networks require to store memories, process sensory inputs, or make decisions.

“Energetics is everything,” Devor emphasized. “Our basic brain activity cannot happen unless the brain utilizes ATP, and we don’t really understand and don’t have a quantitative account of how much ATP different types of computations in the brain utilize.”.

One of the central mysteries SCOBE investigators will tackle is a metabolic shift known as aerobic glycolysis. Under baseline resting conditions, brain cells burn glucose efficiently using oxygen inside mitochondria—the cell’s high-yield power stations. However, the moment neurons become actively engaged in a demanding cognitive task, the brain abruptly begins consuming far more sugar than can be oxidized by mitochondria, routing glucose through rapid, mitochondria-independent glycolysis.

Devor highlights two primary hypotheses driving this phenomenon:.

Industry observers note that “These ideas are not new, but testing it experimentally requires new research tools and quantitative models. Our SCOBE consortium is perfectly positioned to deliver both,” Devor noted.

In a recent development, furthermore, the team will investigate the upstream chemical switches that turn up this metabolic dial during moments of focus and alertness. Researchers suspect that norepinephrine, a neuromodulator closely related to adrenaline that heightens arousal and cognitive acuity, directly triggers rapid glycolysis upregulation to meet sudden computational loads.

Because the brain lacks substantial internal fuel reserves, it depends on continuous vascular delivery of glucose and oxygen. Consequently, even microscopic disruptions, such as blood flow stoppages in single capillaries, can starve local neurons. Such capillary dysfunction and silent microstrokes are pervasive features of biological aging and neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimer’s disease.

Paradoxically, clinical and experimental studies have also documented remarkable instances where neurons recover full cellular function following prolonged periods of oxygen deprivation, suggesting the brain possesses hidden metabolic survival mechanisms that remain poorly understood.

Unraveling these residual metabolic pathways could yield major breakthroughs in emergency medicine, guiding improved neuroprotective protocols for resuscitation following cardiac arrest or acute ischemic stroke.

Backed by the Simons Foundation’s 10-year funding horizon, double the duration of standard federal grants, and dedicated high-performance computational infrastructure to share massive neurophotonic imaging datasets across partner labs in the U.S., Norway, and Austria, SCOBE aims to build the first comprehensive energetic blueprint of the thinking brain.

What is the Simons Collaboration on Brain Energetics (SCOBE)?

SCOBE is a 10-year international research consortium comprising 26 labs across the US and Europe, co-led by Anna Devor (Boston University) and Tom Clandinin (Stanford University). Its goal is to quantify the exact energy (ATP) costs of brain computation from the molecular level up to complex behavior.

Why does the brain switch to inefficient energy production when thinking hard?

During active cognitive tasks, the brain consumes extra sugar using glycolysis, a process that yields less ATP per sugar molecule than mitochondria, but operates much faster. Researchers are testing whether the brain trades efficiency for speed, or whether supportive glial cells consume this sugar to fuel active neurons.

How could mapping brain energetics improve medical treatments?

Understanding how brain cells produce energy and survive temporary oxygen shortages could lead to better treatments for stroke, microvascular aging, and neurodegenerative diseases, while improving emergency resuscitation strategies after cardiac arrest.

How to Deal With the Grief of an Aging Body

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Body changes can raise disturbing feelings, such as looking in a mirror and seeing a reflection that may feel spiritually empty, unproductive, ugly, or weak.
  • Industry observers note that unpleasant sensations such as pain, pins and needles, soreness coursing through limbs, and an inexplicable fog filling the head are a reminder that this body is not the same you anymore, prompting us to wish there was a way to get back there.
  • This is the disillusionment that most of the population will face at some point in life, through aging, chronic pain, or invisible illness (a disease or health problem that cannot be externally seen, including autoimmune diseases, chronic pain and fatigue, and recently, long COVID).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Body changes can raise disturbing feelings, such as looking in a mirror and seeing a reflection that may feel spiritually empty, unproductive, ugly, or weak.

Industry observers note that unpleasant sensations such as pain, pins and needles, soreness coursing through limbs, and an inexplicable fog filling the head are a reminder that this body is not the same you anymore, prompting us to wish there was a way to get back there. It may feel impossible to live well unless you do.

This is the disillusionment that most of the population will face at some point in life, through aging, chronic pain, or invisible illness (a disease or health problem that cannot be externally seen, including autoimmune diseases, chronic pain and fatigue, and recently, long COVID).

Industry observers note that recent global estimates suggest one in five people are at the moment experiencing chronic pain. The most prevalent chronic pain reported by adults ages 75 and over includes low back pain and migraine, while tension-type headaches are more often experienced by younger adults. Chronic illness (diabetes, heart disease, and other mid-to-late-life diagnoses) affects about three-quarters of the world population.

Despite how common chronic illness is worldwide, the nuances of navigating a changing body are not often discussed. It’s time for an honest, evidence-based conversation about what it means to navigate chronic pain and illness, aging and transforming identity post-diagnosis, and how to grieve this loss and maintain meaning through these changes.

Research suggest that those with internalized stigma of chronic illness are more preoccupied with how their illness detracts from their view of themselves, and also have a greater tendency to overlook positive aspects of life with a chronic illness.

In a recent development, psychologists have observed how preoccupation with illness or pain is often accompanied by other grief behaviors. A 2025 study explored how Danish chronic illness patients navigated loss and growth. The study found that many with chronic illness find themselves mourning the life that they thought they would have, often leading to loss of motivation and joy in everyday life.

The perception of losing the life they had once envisioned is often accompanied by a focus on getting back to the “before illness” version of themselves as people struggle to accept how their body has changed, perhaps in how it looks but definitely in how it feels.

Industry observers note that these changes and associated feelings of loss often permeate a person’s sense of identity, as well as their perceived roles within social relationships. Many report a fear of burdening others, especially loved ones, often describing feelings of guilt that “others have it worse than I do.” This is where internalized stigma festers.

Some people have also described feelings of anger, isolation, shame, and exhaustion accompanying sadness. Meanwhile, others have expressed frustration over a gradual loss rather than a “clean break,” accompanied by the inability to find closure.

First, it’s notable to understand why accepting this continuous loss feels so impossible. Theories of control in psychology state that humans desire control or the ability to achieve a desired outcome according to our own standards.

The best and most enduring of our articles, podcasts, and videos about getting older.

In a recent development, when that ability is seen as stripped away, people are more likely to experience negative mental health symptoms, like anxiety, depression, and even grief. Specifically, feelings of diminished perceived control (subjective belief about our ability to achieve desired outcomes) occur when we face continuous roadblocks to living our desired life because of chronic illness.

Industry observers note that one of the major consequences of loss and major life change is that it can disrupt meaning and challenge identity, purpose, and assumptions about the future. At a time when people feel there is little they can control, psychologist Robert Neimeyer’s Meaning Reconstruction Theory poses the questions: “How do I move forward?” and “What matters most?”.

Recent findings suggest that while the original theory was proposed as an approach to coping with the loss of a loved one, the process is somewhat similar to grieving the close ally that is your body. This theory approaches grief by making sense of the loss and finding ways to rebuild a sense of purpose in a changed life (and body).

To answer relevant questions about how to move forward with chronic illness, two ongoing approaches are needed: integrating the loss and recentering purpose and meaning.

Integrating the loss may look like processing significant bodily losses in therapy, finding trusted loved ones to talk about the loss with, and focusing on being realistic about your current body without judgment.

Sources indicate that second, recentering purpose during this major life change involves understanding your why: why is this loss so significant to you, why does it hurt? Maybe it’s because you love hiking in the mountains and a upcoming diagnosis with arthritis feels like the end of this joy. Part of rebuilding meaning is finding new approaches to fulfilling this purpose—perhaps hiking may look different, but nature can be accessed and loved with chronic illness present.

Industry observers note that rebuilding meaning might also look like making meaning from this loss: What has this change taught you about yourself, about the impact you can make? Approaching present and future with this perspective helps process grief in a more protective way.

Living with chronic pain, illness, and the changes that come with aging often involves grieving physical loss, but also shifts in purpose, relationships, identity, and future plans. While these changes challenge our perceived control and purpose, the Meaning Reconstruction Theory suggests that acceptance and growth comes with integrating loss and rebuilding purpose alongside these changes.

Although the present is different than anticipated, fulfillment is still possible with your current body.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shanghai is a restless city. Its impatient hustle may spare its art scene from the plateau of middle age as it navigates a crisis of transition after the Covid years derailed its late 2010s momentum. Going into Shanghai’s annual art week (10-15 November), with two established fairs anchoring an explosion of art events across the city, its galleries, artists and institutions are assessing how the city’s art market can weather China’s economic slowdown and whether the cultural momentum of the past three decades can be sustained.

In a recent development, “Shanghai has so many galleries, so many museums, so many eccentric little spaces that you could come in the middle of summer and still see art non-stop,” says Lorenz Helbling, who founded ShanghArt in 1996. One of the first contemporary art galleries in China, it now has locations in Shanghai, Beijing and Singapore. The Swiss transplant says the volume of artistic activity in the city of 25 million people can be compared to Newly introduced York’s, though the scene can be harder to find. “You can make a lot of fun things here.”.

The city’s two large-scale fairs, Art021 Shanghai (11-14 November) and West Bund Art & Design (10-15 November), established in 2013 and 2014 respectively, set the barometer and prime the mood. So far, Shanghai’s core galleries have largely survived China’s property crash and deflationary economy, but they need young artists and latest collectors to continue buoying their businesses.

Sources indicate that lise Li, who founded Shanghai’s Vanguard Gallery in 2004, states the city is “still in an upward phase, just growing much more slowly than before”. During art week, Li’s gallery will participate in the second iteration of the boutique fair Hangover Shanghai (11-15 November) and in Art021, while showing the artist Tang Chao in the gallery and collaborating on a group show at the artist-run 33ml Offspace. Several artists represented by Vanguard are having big moments nearby: Liao Fei will simultaneously be showing at Hangzhou’s Imagokinetics and the artist group known as Jiū Society has an exhibition at Nanjing’s Beiqiu Museum of Contemporary Art.

Established in 2013, Art021 Shanghai (pictured in 2025) is one of the most successful art fairs in the city Photo: Lisa Movius.

Though the buzz of the 2010s has quieted, Li claims, “there are quite a few more art institutions, and more newcomers are getting involved. The number of young artists is increasing rapidly; we see a lot of fresh faces every year. But most exhibitions are relatively conservative, which is rather a pity.”.

In a recent development, the market has “changed considerably” compared to what now “might be called the ‘golden 15 years’ of China’s contemporary art market: the shift in the broader economic environment over the past few years has been impossible to ignore”, Otto Neu says. In 2022 he co-founded Nan Ke Gallery, which has a group show about art and literature on view during the fair week. “For artists and galleries alike, it is certainly a challenging moment. We probably have to work twice as hard as we did before simply to survive and keep things moving.”.

It has been revealed that change, Neu adds, does not have to be negative. He cites the Chinese expression “great waves wash away the sand and leave the gold behind”, adding that “difficult periods can force an industry to become more focused, more rigorous and perhaps more honest about what really matters. In that sense, this may also be an key stage of maturation for Shanghai’s art scene.”.

In a recent development, in addition to this month’s two international art fairs, Shanghai’s many resident artists—ranging from established figures like Ding Yi, Zhang Enli and Yang Fudong to mid-career and emerging talents—can rely on year-round programming at a healthy variety of homegrown and imported galleries. Western outfits like Almine Rech, Perrotin and Lisson maintain spaces in Shanghai, as do Asian powerhouses including Japan’s Ota Fine Arts and Korea’s Arario Gallery. ShanghArt has been joined by several influential local galleries, among them Antenna Space, Gallery Vacancy, Capsule Gallery and Don Gallery.

According to recent reports, major state-backed museums like the Power Station of Art, Museum of Art Pudong and West Bund Museum (which is partnered with the Centre Pompidou in Paris) have a complement of private museums that have proliferated since the 2010s. The Rockbund Art Museum, Long Museum and Yuz Museum are the best known, but smaller, newer, specialised or further-flung institutions like Fotografiska and the Museum of Glass, and non-profit spaces like Pond Society, Longlati and Prada Rong Zhai, have also enriched the Shanghai art ecosystem.

Sources indicate that vanguard Gallery’s Li credits Shanghai’s “open-city vibe” and its large base of collectors and visitors, along with the museums, galleries and artists, plus a citizenry curious “about fashion and new things, a strong history of business, and a diverse cultural structure. The main downside is that the cost of living is too high.” The lack of art information platforms, even in Chinese, is the other main challenge, she indicates.

The sense of openness is what drew the collector Cherry Xu to open her art-meets-fashion space Cheruby in the city last year. With newly introduced initiatives, “the boundaries between artists, designers, musicians and people working in fashion are becoming increasingly blurred”, she says, opening the art world to new audiences. “This kind of natural crossover between different fields is something very particular to Shanghai,” Xu says. “Art here doesn’t operate as an isolated system; it is constantly in conversation with design, music, fashion, technology and a broader youth culture, with these different communities influencing one another.”.

Recent findings suggest that compared to Beijing’s art scene, Neu notes, Shanghai’s creative community maintains a “healthy sense of distance. There is a certain independence between galleries, institutions, artists and collectors, which has shaped a rather distinctive ecosystem here”, a happy, pragmatic chaos of sorts. Beijing’s art scene is built on personal connections, Neu says, while in Shanghai, “between institutions, between galleries and even between galleries and collectors, there is often an understanding that business is business, friendship is friendship, and collaboration does not necessarily require complicated personal obligations or relationships”.

Recent findings suggest that however, Neu adds that those divisions could become vulnerabilities in the current economic upheaval. “Perhaps this is precisely the moment when Shanghai’s art community needs to become a little more connected and cohesive than it has been in the past—not by giving up its independence, but by finding better ways to support one another,” he notes.

Helbling notes that Beijing is “more split up into scenes which work on their own”, while Shanghai has various circles that interact and are more permeable. He likens the city’s art community to its fairly compact geography, with the art neighbourhoods all within comparably easy reach of each other.

Industry observers note that twenty years ago, Shanghai was the upstart artistic challenger to Beijing, the political capital home to China’s leading art academy. Hong Kong’s concurrent cultural rise proved complimentary to Shanghai’s, and many in Shanghai say the expanding art activity in Korea, Japan and Singapore—as well as in mainland Chinese cities like Chengdu, Shenzhen and nearby Nanjing, Hangzhou and Suzhou—have been net positives for the local scene.

“This situation didn’t happen overnight; it’s the result of years of collaboration between Shanghai’s art institutions, galleries and fairs, as well as the collectors and artists living here,” Li notes. “It’s not simply due to fairs or art weeks alone. The rise of art in latest Chinese cities has also become developed, likely influenced by Shanghai and Hong Kong.”.

Industry observers note that shanghai “was one of the earliest cities in China to develop a contemporary art market, and its relatively open culture and international outlook have given it a particular advantage”, Neu says. “Whether we are talking about collecting, aesthetic awareness or public understanding of contemporary art, Shanghai has accumulated more than two decades of experience and audience development. That kind of cultural infrastructure takes time to build.”.

Recent findings suggest that he adds that growing art scenes in other mainland cities represent “something very positive for Shanghai rather than a threat. A stronger regional art ecosystem ultimately creates more audiences, more conversations and more opportunities for everyone. Healthy competition and exchange between cities can only make the broader Chinese art scene more dynamic.”.

Regionally, Xu indicates, Shanghai “has a very distinct local culture, its own audiences and creative communities, [while] its relationship with other Asian cities is becoming much more direct. It feels increasingly natural for artists, curators and other creative practitioners to live and work across different cities in Asia, and for us to look to what is happening in Tokyo, Seoul, Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok and elsewhere in the region, rather than instinctively treating Europe and the US as the only points of reference.” For Shanghai’s art week, Cheruby is showing a solo exhibition by the multidisciplinary Thai artist Tanat Teeradakorn.

“Shanghai has an interesting place within this network,” Xu says. “It has a relatively mature art infrastructure, but also very strong fashion, design, commercial, technological and popular cultures, and these worlds exist very close to one another in everyday life. It also has a large and increasingly young audience, so when an artist comes to Shanghai, they are encountering more than an established ‘art world’; they are entering a complex and fast-moving urban environment that is constantly being reshaped by newly introduced forms of consumption, technology and youth culture. That complexity creates a lot of possibilities.”.

Zhang Ruyi, whose 2022 exhibition at Beijing’s UCCA Center for Contemporary Art is shown here, is among Shanghai’s mid-career artists to watch Photo: Sun Shi; courtesy UCCA Center for Contemporary Art.

Industry observers note that after helping to build the careers of some of Asia’s biggest art stars, Helbling now focuses on cultivating rising talents through more group shows and dialogue. “You always look at what artists are doing,” he says. “Many of them now operate between here and the West—educated here and in the West”, with networks and roots in both cultures.

Sources indicate that after suspended mobility during the Covid years, dual-culture artists in Shanghai and across Asia have resumed their frequent travels between regions. Often the children of artists or collectors, young Chinese artists are very well versed in both Western and Asian artistic traditions, giving them a sophisticated perspective. “They have an interesting job to do to figure out what kind of art makes sense today,” Helbling states.

He recalls the “loneliness” of Shanghai’s 1990s avant-garde, now rendered “impossible” by contemporary art’s citywide popularity. Still, he views the 2000 internationalisation of the Shanghai Biennale, the first contemporary art fair SH Contemporary (2007-14), and the flowering of galleries and museums as all part of one era.

“There was from the 1990s when Shanghai opened up until the Covid time, and there is after Covid time,” he says. “The first 30 years, and now the second 30 years.”.
