How Do You Raise Kids to Be Emotionally Mature?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting.
  • While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.
  • According to recent reports, according to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting. During these years, it’s easy to prioritize your child’s grades, sports, and other accolades, especially as they inch toward leaving the nest.

While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.

According to recent reports, according to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers. Research shows emotional maturity is the ability to accept and express care, temper major feelings, and make wise choices. Without it, teens are more likely to feel lonely and less satisfied with life, one study found.

In her latest book, How to Raise an Emotionally Mature Child, Gibson points out that “the quality of humanity’s future depends on the emotional maturity of coming generations.”.

Recent findings suggest that juli Fraga: In your book, you mention that humanity’s future will depend on emotional maturity. Why does this matter so much right now?

Lindsay Gibson: Emotional maturity is critical to our well-being as individuals and to the smooth, productive, and innovative aspects of society. When you’re emotionally mature, you can think and anticipate consequences. You can also look back and learn from what you’ve done before. So, you can rely on your thinking to help you deal with reality. Emotional maturity also means tuning into your inner world, including your emotions, imagination, hopes, dreams, connections to other people, and sense of belonging.

In a recent development, JF: Our society places a lot of emphasis on achievement, and less importance on emotional intelligence. How can parents help their teens balance the two?

In a recent development, LG: There’s a real cultural pull in society to prize intelligence and achievement. But when parents get too fixated on these qualities, a child may feel like performance matters more than their thoughts, feelings, and sense of safety.

Recent findings suggest that kids need to be safely held and supported through the growing-up process. It helps them feel resilient, secure, and confident—qualities they need to take out into the world to function independently. If you get too fixated on the intelligence and achievement parts, you’ve got someone who’s very powerful in one area, but whose emotional side may be underdeveloped. It’s the balance between the two that matters.

Sources indicate that JF: In your book, you mention why it’s so important for parents to help their kids develop a sense of self. Can you explain why this matters, especially during the teen years when kids are individuating?

LG: One way teens find out who they are is by discovering who they’re not. Teens might push a limit or break a rule, and it’s all par for the course. What’s notable for parents is to be able to recognize and imagine that their child has a separate heart and mind from theirs—a process called “mentalization.”.

Recent findings suggest that A self is that inner spark that speaks to us. It says “don’t do that” or “now’s the time to go for it.” It guides you toward what’s most compatible with your individuality and who you are meant to be.

Our sense of self comes from our relationships with people we love and who love us. To feel secure, kids need solid, dependable, connected, and deeply resonant relationships with their parents and caretakers. They need parents who are curious and reflect something back that’s meaningful about who the young person is. When they have that foundation, they have a sense of being a real person inside.

It has been revealed that JF: Parents are so busy these days, and overloaded—mentally and emotionally. Raising emotionally mature kids may feel like another big to-do on an already long list. What advice do you have?

LG: Taking time to pause and take your child seriously as a real person will work wonders for their self-confidence and future resilience.

Slowing down takes practice because by the time you’re old enough to have a family, you’ve probably been very goal-directed; parents can be pretty hard on themselves because our culture is so fixated on achievement.

But pulling yourself away from your goal for even a second to tend to your child is something worth practicing because that’s what children’s needs are all about. Kids also develop confidence when they know they matter just as much as anybody else.

JF: What are some behaviors that are normal for teens but that parents might misinterpret as pushback or misbehavior?

LG: Sometimes teens experiment with saying or doing things that clash with their socialization up to that point, such as the language they use or the clothes they wear. These are things that the parent can feel like, “Whoa, I’m uncomfortable with this…”.

Here are two meaningful ways to navigate these moments.

Ask your teen questions about what they’re into, such as the styles they like or what they admire about someone they idolize. Try showing interest, not intrusive interest, but just interest in what they like, or why they are experimenting with different things.

Keep in mind that when your teen snaps at you, is in a bad mood, or slams the door, their emotional centers are activated in a way that will probably never be repeated in their life because their brains prioritize emotional development first during this stage.

JF: Can you share more about why a teen’s development follows this trajectory?

LG: Yeah, I know it’s easy to ask, “Why in the world would nature do it that way?” It’s because that’s how important the emotional self and relationships are to our real success as independent adults.

As adults, we have to know ourselves inside and out and use our feelings to guide us. Teens are still trying to work this out. Learning how to handle these emotions takes a lot of practice. They’re finding out what it’s like to feel rage, or what it’s like to be in love, or to feel disappointed. And they’re feeling them in the most intense way they ever will, because the brain is taking on the job of developing them into a really deep, complete human being.

JF: What advice do you have for parents when their teen’s emotions push their own buttons?

LG: Keep in mind that when your teen responds in an adamant, emotional, defiant way, or calls you names, they’re not really in command of those emotions yet.

Instead of coming down hard with words that suggest they’re not a good person, try to respond with: “I’m really interested in how you feel about this. I want to hear your arguments, but when you call me a name, it makes it impossible for me to be available to you. It just doesn’t work. We don’t call each other names in this family. That won’t work when you’re an adult, either.”.

The interaction then becomes an education about how people respond to different kinds of approaches. Harshness that stops a teen cold shuts down their impulse to communicate their feelings to other people, which isn’t good for resilience or honest relationships.

JF: What are two things that parents do to foster emotional maturity that can actually backfire?

LG: One is the importance of achievement, of having a good resume. Of course, parents know how hard life is as an adult. We feel it’s our duty to convey these realizations to our kids. But when it becomes something that feels like everything else will fall into place if you do these things first or achieve X, we are not helping our kids with the emotional or interpersonal side of life. We’re creating a one-dimensional kind of person.

Sometimes parents also think that if they don’t give their child severe consequences or punishments, the child won’t learn and mature. When you try to convey information through punishment, you actually teach a child to defer to other people’s anger and control. Of course, we want them to be aware of consequences, but sometimes we can go too far. You can’t have a full, right life if you’re always anticipating that somebody might be mad at you.

Juli Fraga, Psy.D., is an AEDP-trained psychologist in San Francisco. She supports parents with kids of all ages. She is also the co-author of the latest book, Parents Have Feelings, Too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

In a recent development, energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

Low energy is the clearest sign of the winter blues among three symptoms studied in young people in the UK, ahead of low mood and losing sleep over worry.

Low mood is also more pronounced in winter, although the difference is smaller.

Shorter days may play a part by shifting the body clock and affecting when young people feel alert, while changes in exercise and social routines could also contribute.

The researchers analysed almost 6,000 interviews with over 4,000 people aged 16 to 24 who took part in the UK’s Understanding Society survey.

They compared interviews conducted in December, January and February with those conducted during the rest of the year, using data from 2022 and 2023 for the main analysis.

On a 0–100 scale, the average score for low energy was about 3 points higher in winter, while the score for low mood was about 2 points higher.

The estimate for sleep lost through worry was smaller and compatible with no seasonal difference.

The figures describe differences between survey reports collected at different times of year, so they give a picture of the group average rather than trace how any one person’s symptoms changed.

Earlier Canadian survey research found that a wider range of depressive symptoms varied by season among young people than among older adults (Lukmanji et al., 2020).

Sleep schedules continue to shift through adolescence and into early adulthood, so the timing of daylight may influence when young people feel most alert.

Winter can also change the shape of an ordinary week, with fewer chances to be active outdoors or spend time with friends in person.

Feeling short of energy could make it harder to stay engaged through a day of lessons or a long shift, even when the person’s mood has barely changed.

The study was published in the journal PLOS ONE (Guan et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

Venice exhibition tells the story of the man who brought together contemporary artists and Murano’s master glassblowers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in 1952, Egidio Costantini, an entrepreneur based in Venice, had a brainwave: to take the designs of contemporary artists and, with the collaboration of master glassblowers on the island of Murano, to make artistic sculptures in glass.
  • Three years later, Costantini established the Fucina degli Angeli gallery to exhibit the results of his experiment.
  • An exhibition opening at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice this month, curated by the art historian Cristina Beltrami, will tell the Fucina’s story from the 1950s to the 1980s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in 1952, Egidio Costantini, an entrepreneur based in Venice, had a brainwave: to take the designs of contemporary artists and, with the collaboration of master glassblowers on the island of Murano, to make artistic sculptures in glass. This was a different approach from that adopted by traditional furnaces like Venini in their decorative glassware, which, although it increasingly involved international designers, was often produced in large, commercially dictated series.

Three years later, Costantini established the Fucina degli Angeli gallery to exhibit the results of his experiment. From then until the 1970s, when other glassmaking companies began to compete, Costantini played a pioneering role in the evolution of glass in Venice, acting as interpreter for more than 100 international artists to Murano’s master glassblowers.

An exhibition opening at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice this month, curated by the art historian Cristina Beltrami, will tell the Fucina’s story from the 1950s to the 1980s. It will also examine the little-documented but vital role played behind the scenes by Peggy Guggenheim herself, whose purchase of many items helped sustain the gallery financially and whose connections enabled Costantini to exhibit his glass across Europe and even in the Museum of Modern Art in Newly introduced York. (As it happens, the collector is also the focus of an exhibition opening this month at the Royal Academy of Arts in London, about her Mayfair gallery of the late 1930s—Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector, 21 November-14 March 2027.).

Industry observers note that more than 100 works, including glass, painting and sculpture, will be on display in Venice, as well as material from the Fucina’s archives, which have never before been studied in depth. These will be exhibited in 11 rooms organised by artist and theme, and will include glass translations of works by many luminaries of the period, from Max Ernst and Oskar Kokoschka to Lucio Fontana and Paul Jenkins.

Peggy Guggenheim among her glass artworks and guests at Palazzo Venier dei Leoni, Venice, in 1964 © Getty Images, by SIAE 2026.

Industry observers note that born in Brindisi in the south of Italy in 1912, Costantini established himself permanently in Venice, where he had been raised and educated, at the beginning of the 1950s. There he became a commercial agent for several of Murano’s glassworks. It was the time of Italy’s post-war economic boom and the city was teeming with creative energy. Costantini seems to have found no difficulty in assembling a group of Venetian artists to form the Study Centre for Painters in the Art of Glass, a collective that exhibited its work at the furnace of Ferro & Lazzarini in 1953.

Sources indicate that the next step was to involve international artists of even greater stature. Acting on his own initiative, Costantini had glass versions made of some ceramic sculptures by Pablo Picasso and then travelled to Picasso’s house in Vallauris, near Cannes, to show him the results. In return, Picasso gave Costantini a copy of the book Faunes et Nymphes de Pablo Picasso (1952). This survives in the archives with markings on the images of ceramic figures that were later reinterpreted as glass sculptures at the Fucina. But who made the markings remains a mystery.

The name “Fucina degli Angeli” (smithy of the angels) was proposed by the French writer and artist Jean Cocteau, a long-term friend and collaborator, apparently in reference to Costantini’s large family. The Austrian Expressionist artist Kokoschka contributed an emblematic sketch of two angels holding up an anvil, which he dedicated to the gallery and its founder, “who first succeeded in making me fascinated with the glass of Murano”.

Max Ernst’s King (Re) and Queen (Regina), both from 1964 © Max Ernst, by SIAE 2026.

Sources indicate that cocteau enjoyed designing extravagant mythological heads for the Fucina, as well as visiting the furnaces and discussing his ideas with the maestri. Both he and Jean Arp, the German sculptor and painter whose work also features in the exhibition, were “seduced by the colour” of glass and its richness, Beltrami indicates.

Sources indicate that the results, though, may not have pleased everyone. The Swiss artist Walter Bodmer allowed his sketch Asymmetric Cat (1955) to be transformed into an oversimplified glass vessel. But after this, for reasons unknown, he never participated again.

The exhibition looks set to offer a fascinating insight into a very personal approach to collaborations between artist and craftsman, as well as an evocative record of an under-appreciated chapter in Venetian history.

• Fucina degli Angeli: Peggy Guggenheim and 20th-Century Artistic Glass, Peggy Guggenheim Collection, Venice, 14 November-29 March 2027.

Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep.
  • It has been revealed that to investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity.
  • Industry observers note that "EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep. Some people can have caffeine late in the day and fall asleep easily, while others may remain awake for hours. But researchers are increasingly finding that simply asking whether coffee delays sleep may miss a more crucial glitch: what caffeine does to the brain after sleep begins.

It has been revealed that to investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity. EEG measurements can reveal much more than how long someone sleeps or how often they wake up. They can also provide clues about the biological quality and depth of that sleep.

Industry observers note that "EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping. Classical sleep assessment assesses sleep duration and its stages, whereas quantitative EEG analysis reveals more subtle changes, such as reduced slow-wave activity, which is an notable marker of sleep depth and its restorative character," explains Prof. Donata Kurpas from the Department of Nursing, Wroclaw Medical University.

Slow waves are a major feature of deep sleep -- the stage associated with physical recovery, replenishing energy reserves, and maintaining healthy brain function.

Caffeine May Make Sleep Less Restorative.

Industry observers note that caffeine does not always affect sleep in obvious ways. A person may still fall asleep at a normal time and remain asleep for what appears to be a full night, yet the quality of that rest may still be altered.

"Caffeine may shorten sleep or make it more difficult to fall asleep; however, even when sleep duration appears normal, it may reduce slow-wave activity and shift the EEG pattern toward a more 'wakeful' brain," notes Prof. Kurpas.

Recent findings suggest that in practical terms, someone might spend eight hours in bed without getting the same level of neurological recovery they would normally expect. Because the disruption may not cause obvious awakenings, it can easily go unnoticed.

"The subjective feeling of having slept well does not always correspond to what we observe in neurophysiological recordings. A person may fall asleep without major difficulty and not remember awakenings, while the brain may display fewer features of deep sleep," the expert adds.

Why Caffeine Affects People Differently.

Sources indicate that another major finding from caffeine research is that responses vary considerably from person to person. Genetics, metabolism, age, stress, and chronic fatigue can all influence how strongly caffeine affects sleep.

For some people, even coffee consumed early in the day may still have an impact by nighttime.

"It is not only about coffee consumed just before bedtime. For some people, the total amount of caffeine consumed during the day and whether the body has enough time to metabolize it before nightfall may also be important," Prof. Kurpas emphasizes.

That possibility may be especially relevant for people who rely on caffeine to improve focus, stamina, or performance, including athletes, people doing mentally demanding work, and anyone who regularly uses coffee or other caffeinated products to stay alert.

Caffeine Can Create a Fatigue Cycle.

Caffeine can temporarily increase alertness and make fatigue feel less noticeable. However, experts caution that the boost may sometimes come at the expense of the body's ability to recover fully during sleep.

In that sense, caffeine can resemble "borrowing energy" from the body. If nighttime recovery becomes less effective, the person may feel more tired the following day and turn to even more caffeine for help.

"If caffeine helps a person function during the day while simultaneously worsening the quality of nighttime recovery, a vicious circle may develop: greater fatigue, greater need for stimulation, and poorer sleep," says Prof. Kurpas.

It has been revealed that these findings are one reason sleep researchers are paying less attention to sleep duration alone. Increasingly, the focus is shifting toward what the brain is actually doing during the night and whether that sleep is biologically restorative.

"Caffeine is neither 'good' nor 'bad'. It is a biologically active substance whose effects depend on dose, time of day, age, lifestyle, sleep quality, stress burden, and individual sensitivity," the expert concludes.

Materials provided by Wroclaw Medical University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#22617. Tech Report: Should We Look to Hunter-Gatherer Societies as Models of Equality?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1071 w)

Tech Report: Should We Look to Hunter-Gatherer Societies as Models of Equality?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that on the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food.
  • Industry observers note that news spreads like wildfire across the camp.
  • It has been revealed that the post-hunt scene above is idyllic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food. Today a Hadza hunter has taken down an animal—a kudu. He can’t carry it by himself, so he cuts his poisoned arrow from its flank, covers the carcass in dry grass to hide it from hyenas, and heads home to enlist help.

Industry observers note that news spreads like wildfire across the camp. Everybody rushes to the kill. They divide up the carcass, carry it back, then divvy it up some more. Every family gets some, and after the meat is cooked, there’s more sharing still. On a good day like today, the hunter and his family retain half, but sometimes they keep much less. People may even walk from other camps, and almost everyone, from miles around, is entitled to a share.

It has been revealed that the post-hunt scene above is idyllic. It paints a quintessential picture of egalitarianism and equality. But our experience as anthropologists working with the Hadza people of Tanzania and with the Tsimane people of Bolivia’s Amazon rainforest is that inequalities are part of even the most equal of societies. Furthermore, the equalities that do exist often emerge from selfish motives.

Insights like ours are revising researchers’ understanding of both the past and how people operate today, as inequality grows globally. Hunter-gatherers are often at the center of heated academic battles about what it means to be human, including debates over gender, war, and peace and whether humans are, by nature, egalitarian or hierarchical.

Sometimes these debates oversimplify. So we pulled together hundreds of different sources covering more than a century of ethnography to find out just how egalitarian hunter-gatherer and other subsistence societies really are.

Anthropologists have called hunter-gatherers such as the Hadza “egalitarian societies,” with equalities of power, wealth, and social status. And it’s true that the traditional subsistence communities we work with successfully limit many inequalities.

In a recent development, most families have similar, modest possessions and store little material wealth. When leaders do emerge, they are highly constrained in how they can direct other people. People often make decisions via consensus, and, if they cannot reach agreement, families will move away.

While the same anthropologists also emphasize that some hunter-gatherers are very unequal and that equality takes deliberate effort, the prevailing impression is that equality characterizes hunter-gatherers, past and present.

A quick trip to your local bookshop will reveal grand claims, including that past hunter-gatherer societies had no permanent leadership and no hierarchy, inequality only spread with the development of agriculture, and humans are noble by nature.

It has been revealed that some scientists are pushing back against these utopian portrayals. The popular bestseller, The Dawn of Everything, calls egalitarianism a “Garden of Eden narrative” that lacks substance. Other scholars have called egalitarian societies a scientific origin myth.

According to recent reports, so where does the truth lie? Probably somewhere in between.

In our recent wide-ranging review of the evidence from the early 20th century onward, we found that no society lacked inequality.

In a recent development, like the Hadza, the Ju/’Hoansi of the Kalahari desert in southern Africa had little property and widespread food-sharing, yet certain families controlled valuable hunting territory surrounding waterholes. The Bayaka of the central African rainforest had little material inequality, yet they bought, sold, and hoarded ritual knowledge. The Philippine Agta controlled and arranged their children’s marriages, hugely discriminating against orphans.

Gender inequalities were commonplace. The Tanzanian Hadza keep certain cuts of meat exclusively for older men, and give more respect to better hunters. Across societies, women have universally done more direct parenting, and men have participated more frequently in community-level decision making.

No society lacks informal leadership. Age was another source of inequality. In many Australian societies, older men controlled ritual secrets and had power over the marriage choices of younger relatives.

Our study also found that although hunter-gatherers are frequently generous, the processes limiting inequality often do not require any generosity. Instead, equality often results from people’s self-interested motives to acquire resources, status, and autonomy.

Recent findings suggest that A great example of this is food-sharing. Although each Hadza family gets a cut of kudu meat, it often happens not because the hunter’s family prioritizes total equality, but because other families request it vociferously. It can involve more taking than giving, often through strongly stated demands or complaints.

Another example is ridicule and mockery of stingy or braggadocious individuals, which keeps greed and bravado in check. Paradoxically, status-seeking can also promote equality, when cooperating to gain status diffuses status throughout the community.

Many of these inequality-reducing processes are familiar to people everywhere.

Sources indicate that ridicule and mockery are ubiquitous in industrialized societies, from political cartoons to social media. Lampooning authority is even common in autocratic societies where governments spend large sums of money suppressing speech. Demands and complaints form the basis of strikes and collective bargaining. And key to social mobility is cooperation among people of different social strata.

It has been revealed that like many great debates, the truth is complex: Our ancient hunter-gatherer ancestors didn’t reach the giddy heights of inequality seen in other societies over the last 6,000 years, but putting hunter-gatherers on a pedestal as paragons of equality is a mistake. Sweeping statements about equality in the past blind us to the tools that probably allowed ancient hunter-gatherers to combat inequality, just as they and people in all societies do today.

Industry observers note that egalitarianism, then, is best seen not as perfect equality but as a set of tools that people use to secure their own autonomy and access to resources. Equality along one dimension or another might be the outcome, but it doesn’t rely on people being amazingly noble or completely lacking in greed or status-seeking. If you consider egalitarianism as equality-creating processes, you can see that it is a widespread reality among hunter-gatherer societies, and beyond.

#22615. Industry News: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

Industry News: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

📅 24 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense.
  • In a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R.
  • The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense. A shadow can briefly resemble a face, or one object can momentarily be mistaken for another. New research suggests that the brain may resolve these visual conflicts by allowing different regions to compare their interpretations until a more consistent picture emerges.

In a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R. Stebbins Fellow Mitra Javadzadeh and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and University College London examined how two neighboring regions of the visual cortex interact. They found that when activity in the two regions matched, the shared pattern persisted. When the regions produced conflicting patterns, however, the disagreement faded within a fraction of a second.

The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.

How Specialized Brain Regions Work Together.

Different parts of the brain are responsible for processing different streams of sensory information, yet our experience of the world usually feels unified rather than fragmented. Understanding how those specialized systems coordinate with one another is a major challenge in neuroscience.

"We are trying to understand how you can have such a high level of specialization between these different blocks, yet always have a consistent holistic outcome," Javadzadeh notes.

The researchers focused on two well known visual processing regions in the brain's neocortex: the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateromedial visual area (LM). Visual processing does not simply move in one direction from one region to the next. Instead, these areas continually exchange information with each other.

Testing What Happens When Visual Areas Disagree.

In a recent development, to explore that communication, Javadzadeh and her colleagues trained mice to tell the difference between two visual patterns tilted in opposite directions. The animals received a reward for recognizing only one of the orientations.

During the task, the researchers temporarily silenced either V1 or LM and watched how the remaining region behaved without its usual partner. The team then used those observations to create an artificial neural network model of the V1-LM circuit. With that model, they could test how the system might respond when particular neurons were altered.

The results revealed a striking pattern. Activity that conflicted between the two brain regions quickly disappeared, while activity shared by both areas lasted longer.

"We find that over time, these types of connections between areas implement a mechanism we call consensus building," Javadzadeh explains.

A Possible Brainwide Consensus Mechanism.

The study examined only two regions involved in vision, but the researchers are now investigating whether the same process may operate more broadly across the neocortex.

"For example, when what you see contradicts with what you hear, do you still use the same kind of mechanisms to reconcile these two?" she wonders.

If dynamic consensus building turns out to be widespread, it could help scientists better understand how the brain combines competing signals into a stable interpretation of the world. It could also shed light on what happens when different brain regions fail to arrive at the same conclusion.

According to recent reports, the idea may even have implications beyond neuroscience. Similar principles could help researchers think about how artificial intelligence systems might handle conflicting streams of information and decide which signals to trust.

Industry observers note that "While we understand individual building blocks of the brain, what is the glue that puts them together?" Javadzadeh asks. "Knowing that can finally help us understand how the brain works as a whole.".

#22614. Breaking: What a Fictional Robot Can Teach Us About Care

Breaking: What a Fictional Robot Can Teach Us About Care

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2123 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.
  • According to recent reports, the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie.
  • Sources indicate that but when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.

According to recent reports, the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie. Josie Joy.

Sources indicate that but when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie. The name was too soft, too ethereal for such a sentient, wide-awake, bird-like baby. I knew that I had to find a new name. Who are you? I whispered into the swirls of her astoundingly warm, circulated, and singularly perfect ear. I couldn’t wait to get to know her.

In another story, a girl named Josie is dying. In Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel Klara and the Sun, Josie has an unknown illness and a prognosis that haunts the pages. Her life exists in the shadow of her sister, Sal, who has already died of the same unarticulated illness, likely caused by an elective genetic alteration procedure known as “lifting.”.

Recent findings suggest that in Josie’s world, being lifted is the new social currency; those who are lifted are expected to have greater access to both intellectual and economic success. The procedure does not, however, come without risk. When we meet Josie’s mother, she is tasked with the impossible: coping with the impending death of her only remaining child. A death likely resulting from a choice she made as a parent. The ultimate consequence.

Industry observers note that klara is a robot purchased by Josie’s mom to be her companion, in part (it is implied) to assuage the guilt she feels. I first read Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun shortly after its debut. Despite being disturbed by some aspects of the dystopian world depicted within, my memory of the novel was poignant. I recalled Klara with particular affection.

Industry observers note that now, the distance between Ishiguro’s dystopian world and our current reality is rapidly collapsing. With the much anticipated film adaptation set to be released this Friday, October 23, and the sudden ubiquity of artificial intelligence in our day-to-day lives, Klara and the Sun is now repositioned as a mirror. If we look closely enough, we might discern what remains uniquely human during this moment of profound technological and social change.

It has been revealed that we are introduced to Klara, the story’s narrator, when Josie’s mom takes her to find an artificial friend, or AF for short. In the novel, AFs confer social standing, but also offer practical assistance—tutoring, companionship, monitoring an ailing child—not unlike the benefits purported by artificial intelligence companies today.

Klara has been patiently waiting, alongside several other AFs, to be chosen. Josie’s mother is the final decider. In a foreboding scene, Josie’s mother commands Klara to reenact Josie’s gait—a test, of sorts—before agreeing to purchase her. It’s the precision of Klara’s mimicry that convinces “the Mother” (as she’s called in the novel) that Klara is the right model for Josie.

Recent findings suggest that all of this, we learn through Klara. Ishiguro’s choice to position the reader within Klara’s perspective allows us to bypass the quagmire question of whether or not Klara is conscious and instead project our own consciousness onto her. In doing so, we view the human world through her sometimes malfunctioning robot eyes, as she nonjudgmentally conveys the complexities of the very flawed and sometimes desperate human behaviors she seeks to understand. In one particularly moving scene, Klara witnesses the vulnerability of caring for another human being:.

It has been revealed that I saw before me, on the near edge of the bed, a large shifting shape, made additionally complex by the patches of blackness and moonlight moving over its surface. I realized the shape was the Mother and Josie embracing. . . . As well as their limbs, their hair had become mingled, and then their shape began gently to rock, in a way not unlike when their goodbyes became extended.

Industry observers note that “Don’t want to die, Mom. I don’t want that.”.

“It’s okay. Okay.” The Mother’s voice was soft, at just the same level mine had been.

In a recent development, prior to this moment, Klara—steadfast and ever-available—had offered her presence to comfort Josie. Yet, despite their far more complicated and at times strained relationship, it is the Mother that Josie calls for.

Recent findings suggest that when I first became a parent, I confided to a friend that when my not-Josie was born, I felt like a fresh sun had burst into my solar system, and I was now orbiting around her. I couldn’t quite articulate the “before,” in my metaphor. I didn’t feel like I was previously my own sun, nor did I feel like I was a planet untethered to others. But there was something distinctly different when she arrived, a whole new consciousness, a space and force and awareness created within me. Her pull was intoxicating, undeniable, sometimes terrifying, and my awareness and attention seemed to expand overnight to now include not only my own experiences, but also to track, perceive, anticipate, and accommodate her own.

If Klara had turned to psychological theory and research about the complexity of parent-child bonds, she would have found a great deal of it. Consider Winnicott’s “good-enough mother” or research indicating that parents and infants are rarely, if ever, perfectly attuned, and the growing body of evidence suggesting that the navigation of the ruptures and repairs themselves reinforce attachment. It has become increasingly clear through evolving applications of experiments such as Edward Tronick’s now famous “still-face” experiment that the imperfect dance between caregiver and child lays the groundwork for resilience and emotional regulation.

In The Philosophical Baby, developmental psychologist and philosopher Alison Gopnik says, “It’s not so much that we care for children because we love them, as that we love them because we care for them.”.

We love them because we care for them.

It has been revealed that beyond Gopnik’s own research, there is an abundance of data to back this up. Studies I have long been familiar with, such as those demonstrating that in same-sex, non-carrying male couples, fathers who act as primary parents show changes in similar brain regions to women who carried their pregnancies and go on to parent their children. Yet, there was something profound about the simplicity of Gopnik’s statement, about love being something we cultivate within ourselves and, more precisely, about care being the means through which we build love, not merely a necessary byproduct.

In a separate interview, Gopnik jokes that spending time with a three-year-old gives you a small taste of sainthood. Not in the sense that the demands are so extreme that you inherently become a saint (though there is a real argument to be made here for any parent who weathers the storm of a parking lot tantrum), but in the actual felt-sense of the divine, the experience of feeling so acutely and utterly in love with this being, so in awe of their singularity, their specialness, their openness to experience, their brilliance.

According to recent reports, gopnik continues on, teasing, about our tendency to claim the uniqueness of our three-year-old, in her case her grandchild, but gently affirms the truth beneath: that there is something numinous, universal, pure within all three-year-olds, a near-magical vitality that we sometimes make contact with when we intimately care for one. Something primal, or perhaps primary, is awoken when we re-experience the world through the eyes of a three-year-old.

It has been revealed that my not-Josie is now three. In many ways she is more unknowable, separate, than she was when she was a newborn, so physically attached and dependent on me. Now, she has her own relationships—with teachers, classmates, family members—that are entirely her own. And yet, she occupies and orients so much of me, continually changing my experience of the world, my access to play, to awe, to unadulterated, intoxicating adoration.

This past summer, I was sitting by a lake, relaxed but hawk-eyed as I watched my not-Josie from the shore. I felt a familiar presence by my side, the barely-perceptible shadow in my peripheral vision of a small body sitting down, and soon thereafter, the unselfconscious weight of a small hand on my leg. I looked down to see a head covered in feathery blonde hair, not the dark, curly brown of my own child.

The wispy tufts belonged to another small child who had clearly mistaken me for her mother. In that brief moment before she looked up, before we both acknowledged our separateness, I felt overcome with the awareness—as though received through the touch of her hand on my leg—that her mother loved her in the way that I love my child, and that, despite how unbelievably special my not-Josie is, my love for her is not. It is precious, but also universal.

Intellectually, of course, this is not a profound realization. Emotionally touching into it is, on the other hand, equally as brutal as it is beautiful. Next to this small child, healthy and safe, I felt her preciousness, but also that of all the children flooding my news feed every day who are not healthy and safe, and whose parents must live with this love and that devastation.

On the back cover, Klara and the Sun is described as a story about love, which it undeniably is. But I think it’s perhaps more fundamentally about care.

Care is arguably more tangible than love, but also more complex, friction-prone, messy. It’s the gaps, the mistakes, the harms, the repairs, the precarity, the forgiving, that make care so deeply painful and so deeply nourishing. Nourishing enough to sustain the vulnerability of love.

Sources indicate that it is care that drives Josie’s mother to have her “lifted” in an age-old attempt of desperation to give her child what she perceives as the best chance at a full life in a rapidly reorganizing world. It is care that sends the Mother down the path of trying to find a way to have Klara “continue” Josie’s life, even though she has already tried and failed to recreate her first child’s consciousness in an artificial intelligence through the work of an artist and scientist named Capaldi.

It is care that allows the Mother—despite her cold exterior—to fearlessly comfort her child as she confronts the possibility of her own death, enveloping her, rocking her, soothing her through the unimaginable. It is the Mother’s human care, not her cowardice, that makes her love true.

There is so much in Klara and the Sun that is undeniably relevant in this particular social, cultural, and technological moment, so many ways in which Ishiguro’s Josie and my not-Josie’s world are suddenly uncomfortably proximate, but it is what Klara herself affirms about humanity that is most resonant.

At the end of the novel, Klara reflects on what she’s learned. She did not have to become a Josie 2.0, for Josie survived. Klara is glad for this, of course, believing that it was her bargain with the Sun (which she sees as a kind of god) that saved Josie. Sitting discarded in a junk yard, Klara is increasingly convinced that the desperate strategy to turn Josie into a digital consciousness wouldn’t have worked:.

Mr. Capaldi believed there was nothing special inside Josie that couldn’t be continued. He told the Mother he’d searched and searched and found nothing like that. But I believe now he was searching in the wrong place. There was something very special, but it wasn’t inside Josie. It was inside those who loved her. That’s why I think now Mr. Capaldi was wrong and I wouldn’t have succeeded.

It is what happens within us and between us when we care for another being that differentiates us as humans. In other words, it’s not so much what’s there but what’s not there—the space between the person in front of us and how we perceive, imperfectly care for, and ultimately love them—that makes us human.

Recent findings suggest that through Klara’s eyes, I was able to see more clearly what connects the Mother and her Josie to me and my not-Josie. It is the very fact that we can so wholeheartedly love another being, without being them, having them, solving them, knowing every bit of them. It is the fact that still, we carry them in our hearts, and somehow we are not heavier for it.

Tech Report: Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coffee may affect far more than alertness.
  • Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.
  • The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coffee may affect far more than alertness. Fresh research suggests that both regular and decaffeinated coffee can alter the gut microbiome and may influence mood, stress, memory, and attention through the gut brain connection.

Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.

The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.

How Coffee May Affect the Gut-Brain Connection.

Scientists have long studied coffee for possible effects on digestion, mood, and overall health, but exactly how these effects arise has remained less clear.

In a recent development, the upcoming research focused on the microbiota-gut-brain axis, the two-way communication system linking microorganisms in the digestive tract with the brain. Signals can travel between the gut and brain through immune activity, hormones, nerves, and chemical compounds produced by microbes.

Researchers examined 31 regular coffee drinkers and 31 people who did not normally drink coffee. Participants completed psychological assessments and kept records of caffeine intake and diet. Researchers also collected stool and urine samples to track changes in gut microbes, metabolism, mood, and perceived stress.

For the study, 'Coffee drinkers' were set as those who regularly consume 3-5 cups of coffee a day, defined by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) as a safe and moderate amount for most people.

What Happened When Coffee Was Removed.

Industry observers note that the regular coffee drinkers first stopped consuming coffee for two weeks. During that period, participants repeatedly completed psychological assessments and provided stool and urine samples.

Industry observers note that when coffee drinkers stopped drinking coffee, researchers observed substantial shifts in their gut metabolite profiles compared with people who did not normally consume coffee. Metabolites are small molecules produced or altered during metabolism, including compounds created by gut microbes as they process food and other substances.

Coffee was then reintroduced without participants knowing whether they were receiving caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee. Half received decaf, while the other half received caffeinated coffee.

In a recent development, after coffee returned to their diets, both groups reported lower perceived stress, depression and impulsivity scores. The findings suggest that some of coffee's effects on mood may not depend entirely on caffeine.

Coffee Was Linked to Changes in Gut Bacteria.

Researchers also found differences in several types of gut bacteria.

It has been revealed that bacteria, such as 'Eggertella sp.' or 'Cryptobacterium curtum', were more abundant among coffee drinkers than non-coffee drinkers. 'Eggertella sp' is thought to contribute to acid secretion in the stomach and intestines, while 'Cryptobacterium curtum' may participate in bile acid production.

Both processes could potentially help create an intestinal environment that discourages certain harmful bacteria and infections.

Researchers also observed higher levels of 'Firmicutes' bacteria, a broad group of microbes that has previously been associated with positive emotions in females.

Decaf and Caffeinated Coffee Indicated Different Effects.

One of the most intriguing findings was that caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee did not appear to affect participants in exactly the same way.

Sources indicate that improved learning and memory were observed only among participants drinking decaffeinated coffee. That finding suggests that substances other than caffeine may contribute to some of coffee's effects on cognition.

Industry observers note that coffee contains thousands of chemical compounds, including polyphenols. These plant derived substances can act as antioxidants and can also interact with gut microbes, potentially influencing metabolism and other biological processes.

Caffeinated coffee, meanwhile, was associated with reduced feelings of anxiety as well as improved vigilance and attention. Caffeine was also linked to a reduced risk of inflammation.

Because the study involved a relatively small number of participants, the findings do not establish that coffee directly causes these changes in mood, cognition, or gut health. However, they provide new clues about the biological pathways that could help explain associations reported in earlier coffee research.

Corresponding author of the study, Professor John Cryan, Principal Investigator at APC Microbiome Ireland, University College Cork, commented: "Public interest in gut health has risen hugely. The relationship between digestive and mental health is also increasingly being better understood, but the mechanisms behind coffee's effects on this gut-brain axis have remained unclear.

According to recent reports, "Our findings reveal the microbiome and neurological responses to coffee, as well as their potential long-term benefits for a healthier microbiome. Coffee may modify what microbes do collectively, and what metabolites they use. As the public continues to think about dietary changes for the right digestive balance, coffee has the potential to also be harnessed as a further intervention as part of a healthy balanced diet.".

The findings add to growing evidence that coffee should not be viewed simply as a source of caffeine. Its many other components may interact with the microbiome, metabolism, and nervous system in different ways.

Industry observers note that "Coffee is more than just caffeine -- it's a complex dietary factor that interacts with our gut microbes, our metabolism, and even our emotional well-being," said Professor Cryan. "Our findings suggest that coffee, whether caffeinated or decaffeinated, can influence health in distinct but complementary ways.".

Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone.
  • Latest research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces.
  • Researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone. The faces that capture a child's attention could provide vital clues about their mental health and how depression develops.

Latest research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces. The pattern appears to differ depending on whether a child has a family history of depression.

Researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time. By identifying these patterns while children are still developing, scientists hope to better understand who may be at greater risk and eventually improve prevention strategies.

"Most of the vulnerabilities that we focus on are still developing during this time period," remarked Brandon Gibb, director of the Mood Disorders Institute and SUNY distinguished professor of psychology. "You can catch things as they're developing, rather than only studying them once they're already there and pretty stable.".

Following Children's Attention Over Time.

It has been revealed that earlier research has linked depression with greater attention to sad faces. However, those associations have generally been modest, and scientists have not been sure whether biased attention contributes to depression or develops because of it.

The Binghamton study was designed to investigate that question by tracking both depressive symptoms and attention patterns over time. According to the researchers, it is the first study to examine how changes in each may predict later changes in the other among children.

"The real novel piece is that we looked at these transactional relations," noted Kelly Gair, a PhD student at Binghamton and lead author of the paper. "Between attentional biases and depressive symptoms, we looked at the way that they were mutually predicting one another across the time points, which is especially novel and hasn't been done before.".

The research team, which also included Leslie A. Brick from the University of New Mexico, followed 242 children and their mothers for two years. Participants were assessed every six months.

Industry observers note that during each visit, children viewed pairs of faces on a screen. One face showed a neutral expression, while the other displayed an emotion (happy, sad, or angry). Eye tracking technology measured which face held the child's attention and for how long.

It has been revealed that children in the study looked at faces conveying different emotions onscreen, and eye tracking technology recorded where their attention veered. Photo credit: NimStim Set of Facial Expressions (Tottenham et al., 2009).

Family History Changes the Pattern.

The results suggest that increasing depressive symptoms do not affect every child's attention in the same way. Family history appeared to play an vital role.

Recent findings suggest that among children whose mothers had a history of major depressive disorder, rising depressive symptoms were associated with greater attention to sad faces. In other words, as these children experienced more symptoms themselves, their attention became increasingly drawn toward expressions of sadness.

"For those who are already at risk, the more these children experience depression themselves, the more they lose their ability to pull their attention away from the sad things around them," Gibb said.

In a recent development, "We know that when you're depressed, it changes what you pay attention to," Gair said. "Our results suggest that these changes may be more long-lasting and may differ depending on family history. One thought is that for children of mothers with depression, who are exposed to more facial displays of sadness from interactions with their mom, these types of facial expressions become even more salient when they experience depression themselves, so their attention becomes increasingly stuck on sad expressions.".

Happy Faces May Lose Their Pull.

A different pattern emerged among children whose mothers had no history of depression.

It has been revealed that when depressive symptoms increased in these children, they did not become more focused on sad expressions. Instead, they paid less attention to happy faces.

"In our lower-risk children, what seems to be happening is that experiences of depression are eroding a protective factor, which is how much they pay attention to happy faces," Gibb noted.

According to recent reports, the distinction suggests that depression may alter emotional attention through different pathways depending on a child's underlying level of familial risk. For some children, sadness may become increasingly difficult to ignore. For others, positive emotional signals may simply become less likely to capture their attention.

It has been revealed that the researchers are continuing to follow the children as they enter adolescence, a period when the risk of developing depression increases for many young people. They hope to determine whether these early attention patterns are associated with a greater likelihood of receiving a depression diagnosis later on.

The paper, "Transactional Relations Between Attentional Biases for Affective Stimuli and Depressive Symptoms in Offspring of Mothers With and Without Major Depressive Disorder," was published in the Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Koto evolves the GoFundMe brand identity around one idea, Help Adds Up, turning the goal bar into a progress circle that radiates outward.
  • Sources indicate that the progress circle is the whole idea.
  • The typeface is GoFundMe Sans, a custom face built for the system, and the specimen sets it substantial on green with letters riding a radial curve.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Koto evolves the GoFundMe brand identity around one idea, Help Adds Up, turning the goal bar into a progress circle that radiates outward.

Sources indicate that the progress circle is the whole idea. GoFundMe's most recognizable asset, the goal bar, becomes a ring, and the ring throws off an arc, a ray, that bends through the entire system. It indicates up as fingerprint-like rings listing real causes, Pacific Palisades Wildfire, Hurricane Helene, Surfrider Foundation, and as words set on a curve. The brief came from a real shift: after acquiring Classy, the leading nonprofit fundraising platform, GoFundMe's product reached deeper into nonprofit giving while its brand still spoke in its early peer-to-peer voice. The palette stays close to the ground: deep green, pale lime, yellow, beige, dark brown. Green carries the trust, yellow carries the energy, and nothing else competes.

The typeface is GoFundMe Sans, a custom face built for the system, and the specimen sets it substantial on green with letters riding a radial curve. That curve is the grid. Words bend along arcs everywhere: Help Fund Give Go! stacked in a bounding box, Change takes action on a yellow poster, And every bit of help adds up curling around a beige field. The voice lines are short and plain, set at a size where the letterforms do the shouting.

According to recent reports, the system lands in the product first. Goal tracking, donation flows, and campaign pages carry the same progress language, and the GoFundMe Pro dashboard turns it into numbers: $28.5k raised online, 227 total donors. Outside the product it holds the same register: a flower macro for the environment discovery page, iPhone screens for the Spring Valley Community Garden fundraiser, campaign photography where the radial type does the talking. The identity also stretches to cover GoFundMe Pro, so the nonprofit platform sits under the same story instead of beside it.
